title: The Pedestrian
author: Ray Bradbury
tagline: Short story · science fiction · a warning about a world that has stopped going outside

overview.intro: In a future city where everyone stays indoors watching television, Leonard Mead is the only person who still walks the streets at night. One evening an automated police car stops him, cannot understand why anyone would be outside without a reason, and takes him away for 'treatment'. The story is short, but it asks a large question: what do we lose when comfort and screens replace curiosity and human contact?

facts.label: Written
facts.value: Early 1950s, when television was spreading rapidly

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: An unnamed American city, some decades in the future (around 2053 in the story)

facts.label: Main character
facts.value: Leonard Mead, a writer who walks alone at night

learn.title: Before you read: the world of the story

blocks.text: Bradbury wrote in the years after the Second World War, when television sets were entering ordinary homes and many people worried that the new medium would make them passive. The story imagines that worry taken to its extreme: by the future of the story, almost nobody leaves the house in the evening because everyone is absorbed in the screen.
A useful way to read the story is as a warning, not a prediction. Bradbury exaggerates a real habit (spending evenings in front of a screen) so that readers will notice its cost.

items: Leonard Mead steps out on a misty November evening for his usual walk. The city is silent and empty; the houses are dark, and through the windows he sees only the grey, flickering light of television screens.
He has walked like this for years without meeting a single other person. The cold air, the silence and the sight of the empty streets are the pleasure of his evening.
A police car appears, the only moving vehicle in the city. It has no driver; it is run by machinery. A metallic voice orders him to stop and asks his name.
The voice asks his profession. Mead says he is a writer, but the machine records him as having 'no profession', because in this world hardly anyone buys or reads books and magazines.

Asked what he is doing out of doors, Mead answers simply that he is walking, for air and to see. The machine cannot fit this answer into any category it understands. It also learns that he owns no television and lives alone.

He is ordered into the back of the car, which is a locked, cage-like compartment. The car announces it is taking him to the Psychiatric Center for Research on Regressive Tendencies, treating his habit of walking as a mental illness.

As the car drives away through the empty streets, the last image is of Mead's own house, the only one on the street with its lights on and its windows open to the evening: a small, bright sign of life in a dead city.

items.meaning: A lonely writer who refuses to give up walking. He is gentle, observant and cooperative, and does not run or resist even when arrested. He represents individuality and curiosity in a society that punishes both.
A driverless, mechanical authority. It does not think or listen; it matches people against a list of accepted behaviour. It stands for a society that has handed judgement over to machines.
Never seen as individuals, only as grey shapes lit by their screens. They are the 'normal' citizens: silent, still and interchangeable.
Everyone has physical comfort but no real company. People sit in the same street without ever meeting. Mead is lonely too, yet he chooses the open air over passive entertainment.
The screen has replaced conversation, curiosity and imagination. Even law enforcement has been given to a machine with no judgement or compassion.
The society treats sameness as sanity. Mead's harmless difference is treated as a disease that must be cured.
The state does not need proof of any crime. Being different is enough, and the 'treatment' is really punishment.

blocks.text: Central idea: a society that gives up thinking, walking, reading and talking in exchange for comfort and entertainment will end up punishing the very people who keep those things alive.

items: Setting as mood: the cold, misty, silent evening and the empty streets create a lonely, almost eerie atmosphere from the opening lines.

Imagery: Bradbury describes the grey, flickering light in the windows so that the houses seem like tombs and their occupants like ghosts. The comparison suggests that the people are alive only in a physical sense.
Contrast: the dark, silent houses set against Mead's warm, lit house in the final image. The contrast between the dead city and the one living home carries the story's hope.

Irony: a man who is doing something perfectly healthy (walking) is taken for treatment, while the people who are truly withdrawn from life are considered normal. The 'Center for Research on Regressive Tendencies' has a name that sounds scientific but shows the reverse of progress.
Symbolism: walking stands for freedom and curiosity; the television for passivity; the police car for cold, mechanical control; the lit house for individuality that refuses to go out.
Simple, restrained style: the plain sentences and short dialogue make the machine's questions feel flat and menacing, which is more chilling than dramatic language.

learn.title: How to use this story in an answer

items: Always say who is speaking, to whom and why before analysing any line from the story.
Use the ending: the lit house is the only detail that suggests hope, so it is a strong piece of evidence for theme questions.
Do not describe Mead as a criminal or a troublemaker. His only 'offence' is walking. The story's point is that the accusation is absurd.
For character questions, link a quality to an action: Mead is calm (he obeys without a struggle), curious (he walks 'to see') and lonely (he has no household or company).

keyPoints: The story is a dystopian warning about screens, conformity and lost curiosity.
Leonard Mead is the only person who walks the streets at night; everyone else watches television indoors.
The police car is driverless and cannot understand the idea of walking 'for no reason'.
Mead is a writer, but the machine records him as having 'no profession' because nobody reads any more.
He is taken to the Psychiatric Center for Research on Regressive Tendencies: difference is treated as illness.
The final image of his lit house, the only one in a dark street, is the story's small note of hope and defiance.
examFocus: Character sketch of Leonard Mead (calm, solitary, curious, non-violent).
Why the title is suitable: a 'pedestrian' is a person on foot, and in this world that is the rarest and strangest thing to be.
Theme: technology and isolation; conformity and authority.
The irony of the name of the Center and of taking a healthy man for treatment.
The significance of the ending and of the contrast between the dark houses and Mead's lit house.
Your view on how far the story's warning applies to today.

vocabulary.meaning: a person who travels on foot; (as an adjective) ordinary and dull
vocabulary.context: In the story, the noun is the key word: Mead is the last true pedestrian in his city.

vocabulary.meaning: moving backward to an earlier or less advanced state
vocabulary.context: The authorities call walking a 'regressive tendency', though it is their own society that has gone backward.

vocabulary.meaning: an imagined society in which life is unpleasant or oppressive, usually because of misused power or technology
vocabulary.context: The story is set in a dystopia where people are controlled through comfort and machines.

vocabulary.meaning: behaving in the same way as everyone else in order to fit in
vocabulary.context: Conformity is treated as normal; Mead's independence is treated as an illness.

vocabulary.meaning: the state of being alone or cut off from other people
vocabulary.context: The citizens live in isolation even though they are separated only by walls.

vocabulary.meaning: a ghost or a ghost-like figure
vocabulary.context: The screen-lit figures behind the windows seem to Mead more like phantoms than living people.

vocabulary.meaning: causing a feeling that something is wrong or illegal
vocabulary.context: In a city where nobody goes out, simply being outdoors makes Mead 'suspicious' to the machine.

vocabulary.meaning: close watching of a person or place by an authority
vocabulary.context: The lone police car patrolling the empty streets is an image of surveillance without human judgement.

questions.prompt: Why does Leonard Mead walk the streets in the evening?
options: Because he has been ordered to patrol the city
Because he enjoys the fresh air, the silence and the sight of the streets
Because he cannot afford a television
Because he is waiting to meet a friend
questions.answer: Because he enjoys the fresh air, the silence and the sight of the streets.
questions.explanation: When the police voice asks what he is doing, Mead says he is walking for air and to see. The walk is his pleasure, not a duty or a search for anyone.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the television option. Mead does not own one, but that is not why he walks.

questions.prompt: Why does the police car record Mead as having 'no profession'?
options: Because he refuses to answer the question
Because in this society hardly anyone reads, so writing is not treated as real work
Because he has lost his identity papers
questions.answer: Because in this society hardly anyone reads, so writing is not treated as real work.
questions.explanation: Mead does say he is a writer. The machine's reaction shows how little books and magazines matter in a world of television.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking Mead lied or refused to answer. He tells the truth and is not believed to have a 'profession'.

questions.prompt: Describe the streets and houses of the city as Leonard Mead sees them on his walk.
questions.answer: The streets are silent, empty and misty. The houses are dark from outside, and only the grey, flickering light of television screens shows in the windows. To Mead the houses look like tombs, and the people inside like ghosts, because nobody moves or speaks.
questions.explanation: Two marks: one for the empty, silent streets and one for the dark houses lit only by screens. Adding the tomb comparison shows you understand the imagery.
questions.commonMistake: Describing a bustling city. The whole point is that it is deserted.

questions.prompt: What happens when the police car stops Mead? Why is the police car described as 'strange'?
questions.answer: The car stops him, a mechanical voice orders him to stay where he is and asks his name, profession and what he is doing outside. He answers truthfully. The car is strange because it has no driver: it is controlled by machinery, and its voice speaks without emotion. In the end it takes Mead away for questioning and treatment.
questions.explanation: Cover the sequence (stops, questions, arrest) and the driverless, mechanical nature of the car. The lack of a human driver matters because it shows that no person is judging Mead.
questions.commonMistake: Saying a policeman gets out and speaks to him. There is no human policeman in the story.

questions.prompt: Why is the ending of the story ironic? Consider the place Mead is taken to and the reason given.
questions.answer: The ending is ironic because a harmless, healthy man is taken away for treatment, while the people who have withdrawn from life into their screens are considered normal. The place he is sent to is called the Psychiatric Center for Research on Regressive Tendencies, but it is the society that has gone backward, giving up walking, reading and conversation. The name sounds scientific and caring; in fact it is a punishment for being different.
questions.explanation: A good irony answer states what is expected (a healthy person is left alone), what actually happens (he is treated as ill) and what this shows about the society.
questions.commonMistake: Just retelling the ending without saying what makes it ironic.

questions.prompt: Write a character sketch of Leonard Mead, giving evidence from the story.
questions.answer: Leonard Mead is a lonely, thoughtful writer who has kept alive habits that everyone else has given up. He is curious: he walks to see the city. He is independent, since he refuses to sit in front of a television like his neighbours. He is gentle and law-abiding, and he answers the machine's questions honestly and gets into the car without a struggle. He is also isolated, living alone and never meeting another person on his walks. His lit house at the end shows a quiet determination to hold on to life and warmth.
questions.explanation: Give three or four qualities and back each with an action. Mention both his strength (independence) and his loneliness.
questions.commonMistake: Calling him a rebel or a criminal. He does nothing against the law except be different.

questions.prompt: 'The Pedestrian' is a warning about technology. Discuss how the story shows the dangers of a society controlled by screens and machines.
questions.answer: The story shows people who have replaced real life with the television. They sit in the dark, grey and silent, and the streets are empty; nobody talks to a neighbour or looks at the night sky. Technology has also taken over authority: the police car has no driver and no judgement, so it cannot understand a man who walks for pleasure and simply files him under 'no profession' and 'regressive tendencies'. The writer's job has lost value because nobody reads. By the end, the machine punishes the only person who is still fully alive. Bradbury does not attack technology itself; he warns against giving up thinking, curiosity and human contact in exchange for comfort. The lit house in a dark street suggests that individuals can still keep a light burning.
questions.explanation: Structure: (1) effect on people, (2) effect on authority and work, (3) the outcome for Mead, (4) a balanced conclusion about what exactly is being warned against.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the story is against all technology. The danger is passivity and loss of judgement, not machines as such.

questions.prompt: Explain why 'The Pedestrian' is a suitable title for the story.
questions.answer: A pedestrian is someone who travels on foot. In the story's world walking outdoors has become so rare that Mead is the only pedestrian in the whole city, and this single fact makes him suspicious to the authorities. The title therefore names both the main character and the simple, harmless activity that the society treats as a crime, so it points directly to the story's central conflict.
questions.explanation: Link the meaning of the word to the plot and the theme.
questions.commonMistake: Defining 'pedestrian' but not connecting it to the story.

questions.prompt: The story ends with Mead's house 'lit up' while the rest of the city is dark. What does this final image suggest, and do you find the ending hopeful or hopeless? Give reasons.
questions.answer: The lit house is the last thing Mead sees as he is driven away. Against the grey, dead houses, its warm light stands for a living, welcoming individual who has refused to give in. This can be read as hopeful: one light is still burning, and it proves that another way of living exists. It can also be read as hopeless: the only person with such a light is being removed, and the house will be empty. A balanced answer would say that the image is a small hope shadowed by loss, and that Bradbury leaves it to the reader to decide whether the light will spread or go out.
questions.explanation: There is no single correct opinion. Marks are given for a clear view, evidence from the ending and recognition of the opposite reading.
questions.commonMistake: Giving an opinion without any reference to the image.

questions.prompt: Do you think the world of the story could become real? Explain with reference to today's use of screens and automation, and to what the story suggests we should do.
questions.answer: Parts of it already exist: many people spend evenings on phones, televisions and games, and automated systems now make decisions about people. The story does not say that machines are wicked; it shows what happens when we stop using our own judgement, curiosity and contact with others. So the practical lesson is balance: use technology for what it is good at, but keep walking, reading, talking to real people and questioning rules that treat difference as a fault.
questions.explanation: Give a personal view, back it with present-day examples, and connect it to the story's warning.
questions.commonMistake: Writing only about how bad phones are, with no link to the story.
